title: Two New NHS Tests Could Slash Endometriosis Diagnosis Time From Nine Years to 45 Minutes
excerpt: NICE has recommended Endotest and Endosure, two non-invasive technologies that can detect endometriosis in primary care, potentially ending the agonising nine-year average wait for diagnosis in the UK.
body:
• NICE has recommended two non-invasive tests — Endotest (saliva-based) and Endosure (gut electrical signals) — for use on the NHS to speed up endometriosis diagnosis.
  • The average wait for an endometriosis diagnosis in the UK currently stands at over nine years, rising to 11 years for women from ethnically diverse communities.
  • Endotest showed sensitivity of 96-97% and specificity of 94-100% across peer-reviewed studies, while Endosure delivers results in approximately 45 minutes.
  • The tests will be used during a three-year evaluation period while additional evidence on effectiveness is collected.

Women in the UK who suspect they have endometriosis may soon face a wait of minutes rather than years for answers, after the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence recommended two diagnostic technologies for use on the NHS.

What the Tests Do

The draft guidance, published on 7 July 2026 and open for consultation until 27 July, clears two technologies for early use in primary care. Endotest analyses a saliva sample for microRNAs — tiny biological markers that can indicate whether endometriosis is likely present. The sample is collected in a GP surgery and sent to a laboratory for analysis.

Endosure takes a different approach, measuring electrical signals in the gut using sensor pads placed on the abdomen. Patients fast for six to eight hours beforehand and drink water during the 45-minute procedure, with results available immediately after testing.

Evidence from three peer-reviewed prospective studies involving more than 1,300 participants reported that Endotest had a sensitivity (true positive rate) ranging from 96% to 97.3% and specificity (true negative rate) from 94.1% to 100%, according to the BMJ.

"These tests are a game-changer because they give us answers much earlier, without the need for invasive surgery, and that means we can start the right treatment sooner."

— Dr Gail Busby, Consultant Gynaecologist, Manchester University NHS Foundation Trust

The Scale of the Problem

Endometriosis affects approximately one in 10 women of reproductive age — around 1.5 million in the UK alone. It is a chronic condition in which tissue similar to the uterine lining grows outside the uterus, most commonly in the pelvis and on organs such as the ovaries, bladder, and bowel, causing severe pain and inflammation.

Currently, the only definitive diagnostic method is laparoscopy — an invasive surgical procedure performed under general anaesthesia that involves inserting a small camera through a cut in the abdomen. The process is costly, carries surgical risks, and contributes to lengthy NHS waiting lists.

A survey of more than 10,000 women conducted by the All-Party Parliamentary Group on endometriosis found that over half had visited their GP more than 10 times before receiving a diagnosis. More than half also reported attending an emergency department because of their symptoms.

The average wait for diagnosis stands at nine years and four months nationally, climbing to 11 years for women from ethnically diverse backgrounds, according to Dr Anastasia Chalkidou, NICE's healthtech programme director.

How They Will Be Used

NICE's recommendation covers a three-year evaluation period. During this window, Endotest and Endosure will be available on the NHS while the companies behind each test collect further evidence on real-world performance. Both tests are designed to support diagnosis, referral, and management decisions — not to serve as standalone diagnostic tools.

They should only be used in women where endometriosis remains suspected despite a normal clinical examination, and must be carried out by a qualified healthcare professional, according to NICE.

A third technology, DotEndo — a blood test measuring biomarkers associated with the disease — was not recommended at this stage, with NICE saying it requires further research.

What This Means for Women Globally

While the NICE guidance applies directly to England and Wales, the implications extend far beyond the UK. Endometriosis affects an estimated 190 million women worldwide, according to the World Health Organization, and diagnostic delays are a global problem. If the NHS evaluation produces strong results, other health systems — including India's, where awareness of endometriosis remains limited — could follow with similar adoption.

For women in the Indian diaspora, many of whom rely on the NHS or navigate healthcare systems where gynaecological conditions are frequently dismissed, faster diagnosis could mean earlier treatment, reduced suffering, and better fertility outcomes.

What Comes Next

The draft guidance is open for public consultation until 27 July 2026. After the three-year evaluation, NICE will review the evidence and may update its recommendations. If the tests demonstrate consistent real-world accuracy, they could become standard diagnostic tools, fundamentally changing how endometriosis is detected in primary care across the UK.
